bracket: [Textbook note — the printed key writes the product as \([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{2-}\), keeping copper at \(+2\). Cyanide is not only a strong-field ligand toward \(\text{Cu(II)}\) but also a reducing agent: it reduces \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) to \(\text{Cu}^{+}\) with evolution of cyanogen, so the species actually isolated is the copper(I) complex \([\text{Cu}(\text{CN})_4]^{3-}\), tetracyanidocuprate(I) — tetracyanidocuprate(II) is not a stable entity in aqueous solution. The answer below therefore names the copper(I) complex. The key's CONCLUSION is unaffected and correct: the complex is so stable that the free \(\text{Cu}^{2+}\) concentration stays below the level needed to exceed the solubility product of \(\text{CuS}\), so no precipitate forms with \(\text{H}_2\text{S}\). An examiner following the book will expect the \(2-\) charge, which is why both are named here.]

[Textbook answer-key error in part (iii): the key lists GEOMETRICAL isomerism for \([\text{Co}(\text{NH}_3)_5(\text{NO}_2)](\text{NO}_3)_2\). That complex is of the type \(\text{Ma}_5\text{b}\) — five identical ammine ligands and one nitrito — and in an octahedron every vertex is equivalent to every other, so wherever the single \(\text{NO}_2\) is placed the arrangement is the same one. Geometrical isomerism is impossible for \(\text{Ma}_5\text{b}\); it first becomes possible at \(\text{Ma}_4\text{b}_2\). The isomerism this complex DOES show is linkage (\(-\text{NO}_2\) nitro versus \(-\text{ONO}\) nitrito) and ionisation (nitrite inside the coordination sphere with nitrate outside, or the reverse), which is what the answer below gives. The key's count of possible isomers is not reproducible without the forms it wrongly admits. Parts (i), (ii) and (iv) agree exactly.]
